name: Marlon
title: Marlon’s outline changes as he turns
script:
Marlon's face looks cleanly outlined from the front. Turn it, and you can see which parts are doing the work.

The short blond hair leaves the temples exposed, while the darker brows frame the eyes. Below them, the cheeks narrow into the jaw and chin.

His jaw scores seven out of ten in this saved Mogging portrait. The three-quarter view adds something the number can't show: how that outline sits in depth.

The cheek contour, jaw edge and chin stop overlapping as much. It's the same face, with more of the shape visible.

name: V
title: What a close-up hides about V’s jaw
script:
Zooming in on V's jaw hides half the story. Pull back, and the cheekbones explain why.

His cheekbones give the face width high up. Then the outline cuts inward toward the chin, giving the lower face that really clear taper.

A jawline close-up cuts that relationship out. You're seeing the edge without the shape that leads into it.

His jaw and cheek area each get eight out of ten in this Mogging portrait. The side view shows why that pairing matters.

At three-quarter, you can follow the transition from cheek to chin. In profile, you can finally see how far the chin projects. Each view adds a piece the first crop was hiding.

Find what gives your own face definition on Mogging.com. Start with the whole shape, from cheekbones to chin.

name: Jordan Barrett
title: Jordan Barrett’s cheekbones need the whole face
script:
Jordan Barrett's cheekbones jump out in a close-up. The side views show why they work as part of a bigger shape.

From the front, the cheek area sits above a narrower lower face. Turn to three-quarter and the contour beneath the cheek becomes easier to follow.

His cheek area scores seven out of ten in the front portrait's Mogging report. That number describes the image; the profile explains more of the relationship.

The nose, lips and chin add another outline entirely. A cheekbone crop leaves all of that out.

name: Tom Holland
title: Prada’s version of Tom Holland
script:
Prada hired the face of Spider-Man and gave him almost nothing heroic to do.

Across these portraits, a crease in the forehead and a glance away from the camera do most of the acting. It feels like you've caught him mid-thought.

His eye area gets seven out of ten in this saved Mogging photo. Put that familiar smile beside the campaign expressions, and you can see how much the mood changes.

Prada's own brief talked about small actions and reactions. The face stays familiar; the performance changes what you expect from it.

See what your own eye area and proportions bring to the picture on Mogging.com, before the styling does.

name: Zeta
title: Zeta’s eyes versus the higher score
script:
Look at Zeta for a second. Which feature did you notice first?

If it was the eyes, here's the twist: his jaw actually scores higher. The eye area gets seven point five out of ten in this Mogging portrait. The jaw gets an eight.

But your first impression doesn't read a scorecard. The dark fringe sits close to the brows, creating a frame around the lighter eyes. That contrast makes the gaze hard to miss.

The fuller lips then give your attention somewhere else to land. Moving between the eyes and mouth, you get a different impression from looking at either feature alone.

That's why the highest score doesn't automatically tell you what will stand out in a portrait.

See where your own eye area and jaw land on Mogging.com. Then look at the whole face, because the highest number only tells part of the story.

name: Clavicular
title: How Clavicular’s new nose changes the facial balance
script:
Clavicular changed his nose. Now look at how it fits between his eyes, cheeks and jaw.

He described a straighter bridge, less width at the nostril base and a slight change in the tip's rotation. Each changes a different part of the outline.

His nose scores seven out of ten and his jaw eight. The interesting part is how those features fit together.

The bridge leads down from the eyes. The base sits between the cheeks, and the tip shapes the transition toward the upper lip. That's why the whole face matters.
